title: Someone tells you they want to end their life
lede: A friend, a colleague, or your child says something that stops you cold — that they cannot go on, that everyone would be better off, that they have thought about how. You are the person in front of them and you feel entirely unqualified.

blocks.text: A friend, a colleague, or your child says something that stops you cold — that they cannot go on, that everyone would be better off, that they have thought about how. You are the person in front of them and you feel entirely unqualified.

items: Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea. The evidence is consistent and it goes the other way: asking reduces distress and opens the door.
They told you for a reason. Ambivalence is almost always present, and the part of them that spoke is the part you are working with.
You do not need to fix their life. You need to keep them safe for now and connect them to help. Those are two achievable things.
The most dangerous responses are panic, minimisation, and a rush to positive reframing — all of which teach them not to say it again.

items.detail: Plainly: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" Not euphemism. Directness communicates that you can handle the answer.
Do not counter their reasons or list what they have to live for. Reflect what you hear. Being heard is the intervention.

items.move: Ask about a plan, means, and timing
items.detail: "Have you thought about how?" "Do you have what you would need?" These answers determine urgency more than anything else.
Ask them to hand over the tablets, the rope, the keys — or agree together to move them. This single step demonstrably saves lives.

items.move: Do not leave them alone if the risk is immediate
items.detail: Stay, or arrange another trusted person, until professional help is engaged.
Crisis line, emergency services, or their doctor. Offer to sit with them while they call, or to make the call with them.

items.say: "I need to ask you straight — are you thinking about ending your life?"
"I am really glad you told me. I am not going anywhere and we do not have to solve it tonight."
"Will you let me look after the tablets for a while? Not forever — just for now."
"I am not qualified for this on my own and I care too much to guess. Let us ring the crisis line together — I will stay on the line with you."

items: "You have so much to live for." It reads as an argument, and they lose arguments to their own head daily.
Promising to keep it secret. Say instead: "I will not gossip, and I may need to involve someone who can help keep you safe."
Shock, anger, or making it about your distress. It teaches silence.
Leaving them alone to "have some space" when risk is high.
Trying to be their only support indefinitely. That fails both of you.
Follow up the next day and the next week, specifically and concretely. The days after disclosure matter enormously.
Help with one practical thing — an appointment, a lift, a form. Practical help lands better than check-in messages.
Get support for yourself. Carrying this alone has a real cost and you are allowed to say so.
Keep the means-reduction in place, quietly, rather than reversing it as soon as things look better.

limit: If they have taken something, injured themselves, have the means in hand, or say they intend to act tonight, call emergency services immediately and stay with them until help arrives. Do not weigh their privacy against their life.
